# SK5002 — Request data reaches a process start

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A value that arrived from the request decides which program runs, or what it is told to do.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Security |
| Default severity | error |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 1.1 |

## Why

`ProcessStartInfo.Arguments` is a single string that the child process re-splits on its own rules, so a quote or an ampersand in the value is not data — it is punctuation in somebody else's grammar, and the result is a second command running as this process's user. `FileName` is worse: it chooses the program. The replacement for `Arguments` is `ArgumentList`, which passes each element to the child verbatim — exec takes an array on Unix, and on Windows .NET does the quoting itself — so there is no syntax left to escape and no shell involved. The replacement for a tainted `FileName` is a `switch` over the programs this code is allowed to run, returning the constant path for each; an allow-list is the only thing that works, because deciding whether an arbitrary path is safe to execute is not a question with an answer. ⚠ There is no fix on the diagnostic: moving one `Arguments` string into `ArgumentList` means splitting a command line, which is exactly the parsing this rule exists to avoid guessing at.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
var file = context.Request.Query["file"];
Process.Start("convert", "-resize 100x100 " + file);
```

Write:

```csharp
var file = context.Request.Query["file"];
var start = new ProcessStartInfo("convert");
start.ArgumentList.Add("-resize");
start.ArgumentList.Add("100x100");
start.ArgumentList.Add(file);
Process.Start(start);
```

## When it does not fire

The rule shares its engine and therefore its whole exclusion story with `SK5001`: a proven intra-procedural flow from a declared source only, a parameter is never a source, and unknown is never a guess. ⚠ The exclusion that matters most here is that argv is not a source, and it is a statement about where the trust boundary is rather than about finding counts. A tool that starts a program at the path its user typed is doing its job; the party supplying argv is the party the process runs as, so there is no boundary to cross and a report would be asserting a vulnerability that does not exist. ⚠ `ProcessStartInfo.ArgumentList` is deliberately not a sink even when what is added to it is tainted: it is the fix this rule recommends, and reporting it would mean telling a reader that the remedy is also the disease. Argument content that the *child program* interprets — a leading `@` or `-` that some tools read as a file reference — is outside the rule, because it depends on a program Skala cannot see.
